# Homographies {#sec-homography}

## Introduction

In @sec-geometry_homogeneous we discussed several types of
geometric transformations of two-dimensional (2D) images: translations,
rotations, skewing, scalings, and we saw that all could be modeled as
the product between the coordinates of a point in the input image
described using homogeneous coordinates and a $3 \times 3$ matrix. Now
that we have discussed camera models, we are well equipped to present a
more general geometric image transformation that opens the door to many
applications: the homography.

As we discussed in the previous @sec-stereo_vision, if we capture a scene with two cameras
from different viewpoints, corresponding points across both images are
constrained by the epipolar constrain. In general, there is not a simple
geometric transformation that maps pixels from one image into the pixels
of the other image. To find that mapping we will need to know the
three-dimensional (3D) location of each point as well as the relative
camera translation and rotation between both images.

However, there are a few scenarios where we can find a simple
transformation that allows warping one image into another image
corresponding to a new camera location without requiring knowing the 3D
scene structure: this will happen when the scene is planar (as in
@fig-illustration_homography) or when the two cameras are related just
by a rotation (@fig-rotation_homography). In those two cases the
coordinates of corresponding points across the two images are related by
a **homography**.


:::{#fig-illustration_homography layout-ncol="2"}
![](figures/homography/IMG_7801_crop.jpg){width="45%"}

![](figures/homography/IMG_7802_crop.jpg){width="48%"}

These two images are (approximately) related by an homography.
:::

interactions.label: Point Depth
interactions.teaches: Varying the depth of the 3D point along the projection ray has zero effect on its projected coordinates, demonstrating why rotation homography does not require depth information.

interactions.label: Camera 2 Rotation
interactions.teaches: Rotating Camera 2 shifts its image plane and changes the projected coordinate mapping, illustrating how homography parameters depend purely on relative camera rotation.

demo_steps.title: Shared Projection Center
demo_steps.narration: Observe two cameras sharing the exact same optical center (the black sphere). A single ray from this center passes through the green image plane (Camera 1) and the red image plane (Camera 2) on its way to the 3D point.

demo_steps.title: Depth Independence
demo_steps.narration: Watch the projected points (cyan dots) on both planes as we slide the 3D point along the ray. Because the ray's direction is unchanged, the projections remain perfectly stationary. This proves rotation homography is independent of scene depth!

demo_steps.title: Rotating Camera 2
demo_steps.narration: Now, rotate Camera 2 relative to Camera 1. As the red plane tilts, its projected point (x', y') slides along the sensor, showing how the homography transformation dynamically adapts to camera rotation.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: An orthographic top-down view looking directly down the vertical Y-axis, tilted slightly to match the textbook's clean schematic style, but fully orbitable in 3D to reveal the underlying planes.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant baseline is the projection ray from the camera center (bottom-left) to the 3D point (top-right), running diagonally at about 20 degrees. (2) Since both image planes appear edge-on as lines and the optical axes are perpendicular with right-angle indicators, the camera is looking directly down the vertical Y-axis (elevation of 90 degrees). (3) The slant of the image lines and the diagonal ray imply an azimuth of approximately -55 degrees to align the origin at the bottom-left and the 3D point at the upper-right.

camera_view.view_notes: Perfect match to the textbook's top-down schematic layout. Users can orbit to see the 1D line representations expand into 2D image planes.

inline_constraints.default_view: Must start as a flat 2D layout matching the original figure crop and labels, letting the user orbit to discover the 3D perspective.
inline_constraints.visible_ui: At most two compact sliders located at the bottom or top edge, maintaining a clean visual field for the geometry.
inline_constraints.explainers: Hover tooltips over the cyan projection points display their homogeneous coordinate formulas.
inline_constraints.framing: Keep the camera center anchored near the bottom-left to leave ample room for the projecting planes and the 3D point.
inline_constraints.camera: Use a clear orthographic projection so that the top-down angle renders the planes exactly as clean 1D lines with right-angle indicators.

interactionPlan.notes: Ensure that as Camera 2 rotates, the corresponding optical axis line, right-angle indicator, and projected point are programmatically updated using standard vector-plane intersections in Three.js.
